chapters.summary: This chapter introduces trigonometry through the study of right triangles found in everyday situations. It establishes the foundational concepts of trigonometric ratios and demonstrates how they can be used to find unknown heights and distances without direct measurement.

<<FOCUS:opposite>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_1:monument_right_triangle>> How tall is that monument over there — without climbing it, without a ladder, without touching it at all? <<PAUSE:long>> It sounds impossible, but you already carry everything you need: your feet to measure distance, and your eyes to measure an angle. <<POINT:adjacent>> <<SECTION:The hidden triangle|id=sec-1>>Watch what happens when you stand on the ground and lift your gaze to the very top of the monument. <<TRACE:hypotenuse>> <<FOCUS:right_angle>> Your line of sight, the ground, and the monument itself quietly snap together into a triangle — and notice that corner at the base. <<WRITE_TEXT:square corner = right angle = ninety degrees|id=text-1>>That is a perfect square corner, exactly ninety degrees, which makes this a right triangle — the star of everything we are about to do. <<POINT:right_angle>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:theta|to=50.0|from=25.0|duration=2500>> Here is the magic of a right triangle: its sides and its angles are not free to do whatever they like — they are locked together. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> <<WRITE_KEY:Fix the angle and one side, and every other side is forced|id=key-1>>Did you see that? As I changed the angle of the gaze, the height was forced to change with it — fix one angle and one side, and the rest are pinned down. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:adjacent>> So if I can stand back a known distance along the ground, and measure the angle I look up by, the height has no choice but to be a fixed number. <<FOCUS:opposite>> But wait — how does knowing just an angle and a flat distance actually pin down a height I never touched? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> Because for any given angle, the ratio between the height and the ground distance is always the same, no matter how big or small the triangle is — and that fixed ratio is exactly what trigonometry hands you. <<POINT:angle_arc>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:opposite_label>> <<SECTION:What the word means|id=sec-2>>And that brings us to this slightly scary word. It comes from three Greek pieces: tri meaning three, gon meaning sides, and metron meaning measure. <<FOCUS:adjacent_label>> <<WRITE_TEXT:trigonometry = measure of three sides|id=text-2>>So trigonometry literally means the measure of three sides — the study of how the sides and angles of a triangle relate to one another. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> From a girl finding a river's width from her balcony, to tracking a hot air balloon's altitude, every one of these puzzles is the same trick: spot the right triangle, measure what you can reach, and let the locked-together ratios reveal what you cannot. <<TRACE:hypotenuse>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_2>>
<<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_2:right_triangle_trig>> Here is a strange fact about a right triangle: the same side can be called opposite or adjacent depending on where you stand. So which is it, really? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> Let's stand at this acute angle, theta. Everything about the triangle's names will be measured from right here. <<POINT:angle_arc>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> <<SECTION:Naming the sides|id=sec-1>>Look straight across from theta. The side directly facing it, the one it points at, is the side opposite to the angle. <<POINT:opposite>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Hypotenuse = longest side, across from right angle|id=text-1>>The longest side, sitting across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. It never touches our angle's corner with a right angle. <<POINT:hypotenuse>> <<FOCUS:adjacent>> The third side touches theta but isn't the hypotenuse. It lies right alongside the angle, so we call it the side adjacent. <<POINT:adjacent>> <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> So watch what happens if I instead stood at the other acute angle. What would change about these names? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> <<WRITE_KEY:Opposite and adjacent depend on which angle you choose|id=key-1>>The opposite and the adjacent would swap. The names aren't glued to the sides, they depend entirely on which angle you choose to look from. <<POINT:opposite>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> Only the hypotenuse stays loyal, because it's always the side across from the right angle, no matter which corner you pick. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> <<SECTION:Building the ratios|id=sec-2>>Now we do something powerful. We take pairs of these sides and divide them. These fractions are the trigonometric ratios. <<FOCUS:opposite>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}|id=eq-1|group=g1>>The sine of the angle takes the opposite side and divides it by the hypotenuse. <<TRACE:opposite>> <<PAUSE:short>> The sine of the angle takes the opposite side and divides it by the hypotenuse. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:adjacent>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\cos A = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}|id=eq-2|group=g1>>The cosine takes the adjacent side instead, again over the hypotenuse. <<TRACE:adjacent>> The cosine takes the adjacent side over the hypotenuse. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\cos A = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tan A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}|id=eq-3|group=g1>>And the tangent compares the two non-longest sides directly: opposite over adjacent. <<TRACE:opposite>> <<PAUSE:short>> The tangent compares the opposite side to the adjacent side directly. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tan A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> Here's the magic: these ratios only care about the angle, not the triangle's size. Sine, cosine, tangent, opposite over hypotenuse, adjacent over hypotenuse, opposite over adjacent. Choose your angle first, and the names, and the ratios, follow. <<POINT:angle_arc>> <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_3>>
<<FOCUS:angle_arc>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_3:special_right_triangle>> What if I told you that you never have to memorize the sine of forty-five degrees, because a single triangle hands it to you for free? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SET_PARAM:theta|value=45.0>> <<FOCUS:theta_label>> <<SECTION:The forty-five degree triangle|id=sec-1>>Here's a right triangle, and I'm setting this angle to forty-five degrees. The three angles of any triangle add up to one hundred eighty. One angle is the right angle, that's ninety. Forty-five is used up here. So the very last angle has no choice but to also be forty-five. <<POINT:right_angle>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> And here's the magic: when two angles are equal, the sides facing them are equal too. So these two legs have exactly the same length. Let's just call each one a. <<POINT:opposite>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> <<WRITE_TEXT:both legs equal, call each a|id=text-1>>Now if both legs are length a, how long is the slanted side, the hypotenuse? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:hypotenuse squared equals a squared plus a squared equals two a squared|id=step-1>>Pythagoras tells us: the hypotenuse squared equals a squared plus a squared, which is two times a squared. So the hypotenuse itself is the square root of two, times a. The hypotenuse comes out to the square root of two times the length of each leg. <<WRITE_EQUATION:AC = \sqrt{2}\,a|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> Now I have every side in terms of a. Sine of forty-five is the opposite side over the hypotenuse, which is a over the square root of two times a. <<POINT:opposite>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> The a on top and the a on the bottom cancel. Sine of forty-five is just one over the square root of two. No memorizing, the triangle told us. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:adjacent>> And watch this. Cosine of forty-five is the adjacent side over the hypotenuse. But the adjacent side is also a. So cosine of forty-five is the same thing, one over the square root of two. <<POINT:adjacent>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:theta_label>> <<WRITE_KEY:sin 45 = cos 45 = 1 over root 2|id=key-1>>That's no coincidence. Because the two legs are equal, sine and cosine of forty-five are forced to be exactly equal. The shape guarantees it. <<PAUSE:short>> Because the two legs are equal, sine and cosine of forty-five are both one over the square root of two. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin 45^\circ = \cos 45^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<SECTION:Thirty and sixty|id=sec-2>>The very same trick builds thirty and sixty degrees. Take an equilateral triangle, where every angle is sixty, and slice it straight down the middle. Here's an example from the chapter. In triangle ABC, right-angled at B, we're told that AB is five centimeters and angle ACB is thirty degrees. We need to determine the lengths of the sides BC and AC. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In triangle ABC, right angle at B, AB = 5 cm, angle ACB = 30°. Find BC and AC.|id=ex-q-1>> To find BC, we choose the trig ratio that connects BC with the known side AB. Now, BC is the side adjacent to angle C, and AB is the side opposite to angle C. The ratio that uses opposite over adjacent is tangent. So AB over BC equals tan C. <<WRITE_STEP:BC adjacent to C, AB opposite to C → tan C = AB / BC|id=ex-step-1-1>> Substituting the values, we get five over BC equals tan thirty degrees, and tan thirty degrees is one over the square root of three. Solving this gives BC equals five times the square root of three centimeters. <<WRITE_STEP:5 / BC = tan 30° = 1/√3  ⟹  BC = 5√3 cm|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now for AC, we use sine of angle C, since sine is opposite over hypotenuse. So sin thirty degrees equals AB over AC. That is, one half equals five over AC. <<WRITE_STEP:sin 30° = AB / AC  ⟹  1/2 = 5 / AC|id=ex-step-1-3>> Cross-multiplying, AC equals ten centimeters. So the two sides are BC equals five times the square root of three centimeters, and AC equals ten centimeters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:BC = 5√3 cm,  AC = 10 cm|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. In triangle P Q R, right-angled at Q, the side P Q is three centimeters and the side P R is six centimeters. We need to determine angle Q P R and angle P R Q. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In triangle PQR, right angle at Q, PQ = 3 cm, PR = 6 cm. Find angle QPR and angle PRQ.|id=ex-q-1>> We start by relating the sides we know to an angle. The side P Q is three centimeters, and P R, the hypotenuse, is six centimeters. So P Q over P R equals sin R. <<WRITE_STEP:PQ / PR = sin R|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we substitute the values. Sin R equals three over six, which simplifies to one half. <<WRITE_STEP:sin R = 3 / 6 = one half|id=ex-step-1-2>> We recognize that the angle whose sine is one half is thirty degrees. So angle P R Q equals thirty degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:angle PRQ = 30 degrees|id=ex-step-1-3>> Finally, the three angles of a triangle add to one hundred eighty degrees, and the angle at Q is ninety degrees. So angle Q P R equals one hundred eighty minus ninety minus thirty, which is sixty degrees. <<WRITE_ANSWER:angle PRQ = 30 degrees and angle QPR = 60 degrees|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We're told that sine of A minus B equals one half, and cosine of A plus B equals one half, with the condition that A plus B is greater than zero degrees and less than or equal to ninety degrees, and that A is greater than B. We need to find A and B. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: sin(A-B)=1/2, cos(A+B)=1/2, 0 < A+B <= 90, A>B. Find A and B.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with the first equation. Since sine of A minus B equals one half, and we know sine of thirty degrees is one half, it follows that A minus B equals thirty degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(A - B) = 1/2  =>  A - B = 30 degrees   ...(1)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now for the second equation. Since cosine of A plus B equals one half, and cosine of sixty degrees is one half, and this fits our constraint that A plus B lies between zero and ninety degrees, we get A plus B equals sixty degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(A + B) = 1/2  =>  A + B = 60 degrees   ...(2)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we solve these two like a pair of simultaneous equations. Adding equation one and equation two, the B terms cancel, giving two A equals ninety degrees, so A equals forty-five degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:Adding (1) and (2): 2A = 90 degrees  =>  A = 45 degrees|id=ex-step-1-3>> Substituting A equals forty-five degrees back into equation two, forty-five plus B equals sixty, so B equals fifteen degrees. And since A is greater than B, this is consistent. <<WRITE_STEP:45 + B = 60  =>  B = 15 degrees|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer is A equals forty-five degrees and B equals fifteen degrees. <<WRITE_ANSWER:A = 45 degrees, B = 15 degrees|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:theta|to=30.0|from=45.0>> That cut makes a right triangle with a sixty degree angle at the bottom and a thirty degree angle at the top, and the base is now exactly half the original side. From those clean fractions, every value for thirty and sixty falls right out. <<FOCUS:theta_label>> So remember the real lesson: these special values are never something to cram. A square cut on its diagonal gives you forty-five, and an equilateral triangle cut in half gives you thirty and sixty. Geometry hands you the answers. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_4>>
Most equations are picky. Take x plus two equals five — that is only true for one number, x equals three. Plug in anything else and it is just false. But some equations are true for absolutely everything you throw at them. <<SECTION:What is an identity?|id=sec-1>>Those special always-true equations have a name: we call them identities. <<PAUSE:short>> And the most famous one in trigonometry is true for every angle from zero all the way to ninety degrees. <<WRITE_TEXT:Identity = true for ALL values|id=text-1>>So where could an equation that powerful possibly come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:theta_label>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_4:right_triangle_trig>> It comes from this — one ordinary right triangle, right-angled here at B, with angle A sitting in the corner. <<POINT:theta_label>> In any right triangle, the two short sides squared and added together equal the longest side squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> You already know the rule that lives inside any right triangle: the two shorter sides squared and added together equal the hypotenuse squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2|id=eq-1|group=g1>>That is just Pythagoras. <<TRACE:hypotenuse>> Now watch one small trick. I am going to divide every single term in that equation by the hypotenuse squared — by AC squared. <<POINT:hypotenuse_label>> If we divide every single term by the hypotenuse squared, the right-hand side just becomes one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{AB^2}{AC^2} + \frac{BC^2}{AC^2} = 1|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:adjacent>> Look at what each piece becomes. The adjacent side over the hypotenuse — that ratio is exactly cosine of A. And the opposite side over the hypotenuse — that is sine of A. <<POINT:adjacent>> Each of those ratios is something we already named: one is cosine of A, the other is sine of A, so the whole thing collapses into a clean little statement. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> And the right-hand side? The hypotenuse squared divided by itself is simply one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1|id=eq-2>>So everything collapses into this: cosine squared A plus sine squared A equals one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:theta|to=50.0|from=25.0|duration=2500>> Here is the beautiful part. We never picked a special angle. Angle A could be anything in the triangle. <<WRITE_KEY:cos^2 A + sin^2 A = 1 — for EVERY angle A|id=key-1>>So this holds for every angle — it is a true trigonometric identity. <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:theta|to=30.0|from=50.0|duration=2500>> Watch the angle change on screen right now — A is shifting, the sides are stretching — and yet cosine squared plus sine squared stubbornly stays equal to one the whole time. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:adjacent>> And the same triangle, the same Pythagoras, can be divided differently — by the adjacent side, or by the opposite side — to spill out two more identities involving tangent, secant, and cosecant. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> So the lesson is really one idea: one triangle, one Pythagoras, and an equation that is true for all angles at once. That is what an identity is — and that is why you can use it absolutely anywhere. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_5>>
<<FOCUS:right_angle>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_5:summary_triangle>> Everything you learned about trigonometry this whole chapter lives inside one tiny triangle, and right now I'm going to fit it all back into one picture. <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> Here it is: a right triangle, with the right angle parked in one corner, and one angle I care about that I'll call theta. <<POINT:angle_arc>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> <<SECTION:Naming the sides|id=sec-1>>The moment you pick theta, the three sides get their names: the one straight across from theta is the opposite, the one touching theta is the adjacent, and the longest one, facing the right angle, is the hypotenuse. <<POINT:hypotenuse>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> <<WRITE_KEY:sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj|id=key-1>>From just those three sides, sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent. <<POINT:opposite>> <<PAUSE:short>> From the three named sides we build the three ratios: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{hyp}},\quad \cos\theta = \dfrac{\text{adj}}{\text{hyp}},\quad \tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{opp}}{\text{adj}}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:adjacent>> And the other three, cosecant, secant and cotangent, aren't new monsters to memorise, they're simply the flips: one over sine, one over cosine, one over tangent. <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> Now here's a question worth pausing on: can the sine of an angle ever be bigger than one? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> <<WRITE_TEXT:hyp is longest, so opp/hyp < 1|id=text-1>>Never. Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, and the hypotenuse is always the longest side, so you're dividing a smaller number by a bigger one, the answer can't pass one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:theta|to=20.0|from=50.0|duration=2500>> Watch what happens to the sides as I shrink theta toward zero, the opposite side almost vanishes while the hypotenuse stays long. <<FOCUS:adjacent>> There's one identity that ties the whole chapter together, and it falls straight out of this triangle. <<POINT:adjacent>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> Pythagoras says opposite squared plus adjacent squared equals hypotenuse squared, and if you divide every term by hypotenuse squared, sine squared plus cosine squared lands exactly on one. <<PAUSE:short>> If you take Pythagoras and divide every term by the hypotenuse squared, sine squared plus cosine squared comes out to exactly one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:angle_arc>> <<WRITE_KEY:sin^2 + cos^2 = 1|id=key-2>>So remember this: sine and cosine never exceed one, and their squares always add up to one, that single fact powers nearly every trig identity you'll meet. <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:theta|to=45.0|from=20.0|duration=2000>> And the special angles, zero, thirty, forty-five, sixty and ninety degrees, are just this same triangle drawn at those exact tilts, with their ratios worth keeping at your fingertips. <<FOCUS:right_angle>> One triangle, three ratios, their three reciprocals, and one identity, that's the entire chapter sitting in the palm of your hand.

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We start from a real human problem — measuring something too tall or too far to reach — and discover that the angles and sides of a right triangle hide a fixed relationship. From defining the trig ratios, to nailing down exact values for special angles, to proving identities that tie everything together, the chapter builds one tool that turns angles into distances.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: How tall is a tree, a building, or a mountain you can never climb — measured without ever leaving the ground? By the end of this chapter, an angle and a single side will be all you need.

coverage_checklist.description: Explain the origin and meaning of 'trigonometry' and motivate it with real measurement problems (heights, distances)
Name the sides of a right triangle relative to a chosen acute angle (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse)
Define the six trig ratios (sin, cos, tan and reciprocals) and show they depend only on the angle, not triangle size
Derive exact values for 0, 30, 45, 60, 90 degrees from geometry rather than pure memorization
Distinguish an identity from an ordinary equation and prove the Pythagorean identities (sin²+cos²=1 and its cousins)
Tie ratios, special angles, and identities back to solving a real height-and-distance problem

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We opened by asking how you could measure a tree, a tower, or a mountain without ever reaching the top — and now you can. The secret was the right triangle: once you fix an acute angle, every side earns a name, and the ratios between them — sine, cosine, tangent — depend only on that angle. You learned the exact values for the special angles 0, 30, 45, 60, and 90 by building them from geometry, and you proved identities like sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 that hold for every angle. Put together, an angle plus one measured length is enough to unlock any unknown height or distance — that's the quiet power of trigonometry.

segments.narration_chapter: Most equations are picky. Take x plus two equals five — that is only true for one number, x equals three. Plug in anything else and it is just false. But some equations are true for absolutely everything you throw at them. <<SECTION:What is an identity?|id=sec-1>>Those special always-true equations have a name: we call them identities. <<PAUSE:short>> And the most famous one in trigonometry is true for every angle from zero all the way to ninety degrees. <<WRITE_TEXT:Identity = true for ALL values|id=text-1>>So where could an equation that powerful possibly come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:theta_label>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:mathematics:introduction_to_trigonometry:8_4:right_triangle_trig>> It comes from this — one ordinary right triangle, right-angled here at B, with angle A sitting in the corner. <<POINT:theta_label>> In any right triangle, the two short sides squared and added together equal the longest side squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:hypotenuse>> You already know the rule that lives inside any right triangle: the two shorter sides squared and added together equal the hypotenuse squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2|id=eq-1|group=g1>>That is just Pythagoras. <<TRACE:hypotenuse>> Now watch one small trick. I am going to divide every single term in that equation by the hypotenuse squared — by AC squared. <<POINT:hypotenuse_label>> If we divide every single term by the hypotenuse squared, the right-hand side just becomes one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{AB^2}{AC^2} + \frac{BC^2}{AC^2} = 1|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:adjacent>> Look at what each piece becomes. The adjacent side over the hypotenuse — that ratio is exactly cosine of A. And the opposite side over the hypotenuse — that is sine of A. <<POINT:adjacent>> Each of those ratios is something we already named: one is cosine of A, the other is sine of A, so the whole thing collapses into a clean little statement. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:opposite>> And the right-hand side? The hypotenuse squared divided by itself is simply one. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1|id=eq-2>>So everything collapses into this: cosine squared A plus sine squared A equals one. <<PAUSE:short>> <<ANIMATE_PARAM:theta|to=50.0|from=25.0|duration=2500>> Here is the beautiful part. hook.text: How tall is that monument over there — without climbing it, without a ladder, without touching it at all?

crucial_facts: A right triangle locks its sides and angles together, so knowing one angle and one side lets you find a side you cannot reach.
Trigonometry means 'measure of three sides' — it is the study of how a triangle's sides and angles are related.

diagrams.purpose: Show that looking up at a tall object from the ground forms a right triangle, where the unreachable height is one side and the angle of your gaze plus your distance are the things you can actually measure.

required_elements.description: the ground distance from where you stand to the base of the monument

choreography.narration: How tall is that monument over there — without climbing it, without a ladder, without touching it at all?
It sounds impossible, but you already carry everything you need: your feet to measure distance, and your eyes to measure an angle.
<<SECTION:The hidden triangle|id=sec-1>>Watch what happens when you stand on the ground and lift your gaze to the very top of the monument.
Your line of sight, the ground, and the monument itself quietly snap together into a triangle — and notice that corner at the base.

<<WRITE_TEXT:square corner = right angle = ninety degrees|id=text-1>>That is a perfect square corner, exactly ninety degrees, which makes this a right triangle — the star of everything we are about to do.
Here is the magic of a right triangle: its sides and its angles are not free to do whatever they like — they are locked together.

<<WRITE_KEY:Fix the angle and one side, and every other side is forced|id=key-1>>Did you see that? As I changed the angle of the gaze, the height was forced to change with it — fix one angle and one side, and the rest are pinned down.
So if I can stand back a known distance along the ground, and measure the angle I look up by, the height has no choice but to be a fixed number.
But wait — how does knowing just an angle and a flat distance actually pin down a height I never touched?

Because for any given angle, the ratio between the height and the ground distance is always the same, no matter how big or small the triangle is — and that fixed ratio is exactly what trigonometry hands you.
<<SECTION:What the word means|id=sec-2>>And that brings us to this slightly scary word. It comes from three Greek pieces: tri meaning three, gon meaning sides, and metron meaning measure.
<<WRITE_TEXT:trigonometry = measure of three sides|id=text-2>>So trigonometry literally means the measure of three sides — the study of how the sides and angles of a triangle relate to one another.

From a girl finding a river's width from her balcony, to tracking a hot air balloon's altitude, every one of these puzzles is the same trick: spot the right triangle, measure what you can reach, and let the locked-together ratios reveal what you cannot.

lesson_plans.title: Trigonometric Ratios: Naming the Sides and Sine, Cosine, Tangent

hook.text: Here's a strange fact about a right triangle: the SAME side can be called "opposite" or "adjacent" depending on where you stand. So which is it, really?

crucial_facts: The names opposite and adjacent are not fixed to a side; they depend on which acute angle you are looking from.
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent.

diagrams.purpose: Show that the side names opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse are defined relative to a chosen acute angle, and build the three core ratios from those sides.

required_elements.description: the side facing the chosen angle
the side touching the angle that is not the hypotenuse
the longest side, across from the right angle

choreography.narration: Here is a strange fact about a right triangle: the same side can be called opposite or adjacent depending on where you stand. So which is it, really?
Let's stand at this acute angle, theta. Everything about the triangle's names will be measured from right here.
<<SECTION:Naming the sides|id=sec-1>>Look straight across from theta. The side directly facing it, the one it points at, is the side opposite to the angle.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Hypotenuse = longest side, across from right angle|id=text-1>>The longest side, sitting across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. It never touches our angle's corner with a right angle.
The third side touches theta but isn't the hypotenuse. It lies right alongside the angle, so we call it the side adjacent.
So watch what happens if I instead stood at the other acute angle. What would change about these names?

<<WRITE_KEY:Opposite and adjacent depend on which angle you choose|id=key-1>>The opposite and the adjacent would swap. The names aren't glued to the sides, they depend entirely on which angle you choose to look from.
Only the hypotenuse stays loyal, because it's always the side across from the right angle, no matter which corner you pick.
<<SECTION:Building the ratios|id=sec-2>>Now we do something powerful. We take pairs of these sides and divide them. These fractions are the trigonometric ratios.
<<WRITE_EQUATION:\sin A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}|id=eq-1|group=g1>>The sine of the angle takes the opposite side and divides it by the hypotenuse.
<<WRITE_EQUATION:\cos A = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}|id=eq-2|group=g1>>The cosine takes the adjacent side instead, again over the hypotenuse.
<<WRITE_EQUATION:\tan A = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}|id=eq-3|group=g1>>And the tangent compares the two non-longest sides directly: opposite over adjacent.

Here's the magic: these ratios only care about the angle, not the triangle's size. Sine, cosine, tangent, opposite over hypotenuse, adjacent over hypotenuse, opposite over adjacent. Choose your angle first, and the names, and the ratios, follow.

equations.explanation_in_words: The sine of the angle takes the opposite side and divides it by the hypotenuse.
The cosine takes the adjacent side over the hypotenuse.
The tangent compares the opposite side to the adjacent side directly.

lesson_plans.title: Building the Special Angles: 45°, 30° and 60°

hook.text: What if I told you that you never have to memorize the sine of forty-five degrees, because a single triangle hands it to you for free?

crucial_facts: The special-angle trig values aren't memorized facts; they're built from two simple shapes: a square cut diagonally and an equilateral triangle cut in half.
For forty-five degrees, both legs of the triangle are equal, which forces sine and cosine of forty-five to be exactly the same: one over the square root of two.

diagrams.purpose: Show a right triangle with a forty-five degree angle so the equal legs and the square-root-of-two hypotenuse become visible, grounding sine and cosine of forty-five.

required_elements.description: the side opposite the forty-five degree angle
the side adjacent to the forty-five degree angle

choreography.narration: What if I told you that you never have to memorize the sine of forty-five degrees, because a single triangle hands it to you for free?
<<SECTION:The forty-five degree triangle|id=sec-1>>Here's a right triangle, and I'm setting this angle to forty-five degrees. The three angles of any triangle add up to one hundred eighty.
One angle is the right angle, that's ninety. Forty-five is used up here. So the very last angle has no choice but to also be forty-five.
And here's the magic: when two angles are equal, the sides facing them are equal too. So these two legs have exactly the same length. Let's just call each one a.
<<WRITE_TEXT:both legs equal, call each a|id=text-1>>Now if both legs are length a, how long is the slanted side, the hypotenuse?

<<WRITE_STEP:hypotenuse squared equals a squared plus a squared equals two a squared|id=step-1>>Pythagoras tells us: the hypotenuse squared equals a squared plus a squared, which is two times a squared. So the hypotenuse itself is the square root of two, times a.
Now I have every side in terms of a. Sine of forty-five is the opposite side over the hypotenuse, which is a over the square root of two times a.
The a on top and the a on the bottom cancel. Sine of forty-five is just one over the square root of two. No memorizing, the triangle told us.
And watch this. Cosine of forty-five is the adjacent side over the hypotenuse. But the adjacent side is also a. So cosine of forty-five is the same thing, one over the square root of two.
<<WRITE_KEY:sin 45 = cos 45 = 1 over root 2|id=key-1>>That's no coincidence. Because the two legs are equal, sine and cosine of forty-five are forced to be exactly equal. The shape guarantees it.
<<SECTION:Thirty and sixty|id=sec-2>>The very same trick builds thirty and sixty degrees. Take an equilateral triangle, where every angle is sixty, and slice it straight down the middle.

Here's an example from the chapter. In triangle ABC, right-angled at B, we're told that AB is five centimeters and angle ACB is thirty degrees. We need to determine the lengths of the sides BC and AC. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In triangle ABC, right angle at B, AB = 5 cm, angle ACB = 30°. Find BC and AC.|id=ex-q-1>>

To find BC, we choose the trig ratio that connects BC with the known side AB. Now, BC is the side adjacent to angle C, and AB is the side opposite to angle C. The ratio that uses opposite over adjacent is tangent. So AB over BC equals tan C. <<WRITE_STEP:BC adjacent to C, AB opposite to C → tan C = AB / BC|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Substituting the values, we get five over BC equals tan thirty degrees, and tan thirty degrees is one over the square root of three. Solving this gives BC equals five times the square root of three centimeters. <<WRITE_STEP:5 / BC = tan 30° = 1/√3  ⟹  BC = 5√3 cm|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now for AC, we use sine of angle C, since sine is opposite over hypotenuse. So sin thirty degrees equals AB over AC. That is, one half equals five over AC. <<WRITE_STEP:sin 30° = AB / AC  ⟹  1/2 = 5 / AC|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Cross-multiplying, AC equals ten centimeters. So the two sides are BC equals five times the square root of three centimeters, and AC equals ten centimeters. <<WRITE_ANSWER:BC = 5√3 cm,  AC = 10 cm|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. In triangle P Q R, right-angled at Q, the side P Q is three centimeters and the side P R is six centimeters. We need to determine angle Q P R and angle P R Q. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In triangle PQR, right angle at Q, PQ = 3 cm, PR = 6 cm. Find angle QPR and angle PRQ.|id=ex-q-1>>

We start by relating the sides we know to an angle. The side P Q is three centimeters, and P R, the hypotenuse, is six centimeters. So P Q over P R equals sin R. <<WRITE_STEP:PQ / PR = sin R|id=ex-step-1-1>>
Now we substitute the values. Sin R equals three over six, which simplifies to one half. <<WRITE_STEP:sin R = 3 / 6 = one half|id=ex-step-1-2>>
We recognize that the angle whose sine is one half is thirty degrees. So angle P R Q equals thirty degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:angle PRQ = 30 degrees|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Finally, the three angles of a triangle add to one hundred eighty degrees, and the angle at Q is ninety degrees. So angle Q P R equals one hundred eighty minus ninety minus thirty, which is sixty degrees. <<WRITE_ANSWER:angle PRQ = 30 degrees and angle QPR = 60 degrees|id=ex-ans-1>>

Here's an example from the chapter. We're told that sine of A minus B equals one half, and cosine of A plus B equals one half, with the condition that A plus B is greater than zero degrees and less than or equal to ninety degrees, and that A is greater than B. We need to find A and B. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: sin(A-B)=1/2, cos(A+B)=1/2, 0 < A+B <= 90, A>B. Find A and B.|id=ex-q-1>>

We start with the first equation. Since sine of A minus B equals one half, and we know sine of thirty degrees is one half, it follows that A minus B equals thirty degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:sin(A - B) = 1/2  =>  A - B = 30 degrees   ...(1)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Now for the second equation. Since cosine of A plus B equals one half, and cosine of sixty degrees is one half, and this fits our constraint that A plus B lies between zero and ninety degrees, we get A plus B equals sixty degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:cos(A + B) = 1/2  =>  A + B = 60 degrees   ...(2)|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Now we solve these two like a pair of simultaneous equations. Adding equation one and equation two, the B terms cancel, giving two A equals ninety degrees, so A equals forty-five degrees. <<WRITE_STEP:Adding (1) and (2): 2A = 90 degrees  =>  A = 45 degrees|id=ex-step-1-3>>

Substituting A equals forty-five degrees back into equation two, forty-five plus B equals sixty, so B equals fifteen degrees. And since A is greater than B, this is consistent. <<WRITE_STEP:45 + B = 60  =>  B = 15 degrees|id=ex-step-1-4>>
And the answer is A equals forty-five degrees and B equals fifteen degrees. <<WRITE_ANSWER:A = 45 degrees, B = 15 degrees|id=ex-ans-1>>

That cut makes a right triangle with a sixty degree angle at the bottom and a thirty degree angle at the top, and the base is now exactly half the original side. From those clean fractions, every value for thirty and sixty falls right out.

So remember the real lesson: these special values are never something to cram. A square cut on its diagonal gives you forty-five, and an equilateral triangle cut in half gives you thirty and sixty. Geometry hands you the answers.

8.1 Introduction
You have already studied about triangles, and in particular, right triangles, in your
earlier classes. Let us take some examples from our surroundings where right triangles
can be imagined to be formed. For instance :
1. Suppose the students of a school are
visiting Qutub Minar. Now, if a student
is looking at the top of the Minar, a right
triangle can be imagined to be made,
as shown in Fig 8.1. Can the student
find out the height of the Minar, without
actually measuring it?
    2.  Suppose a girl is sitting on the balcony
of her house located on the bank of a
river.  She is looking down at a flower
pot placed on a stair of a temple situated
nearby on the other bank of the river.
A right triangle is imagined to be made
in this situation as shown in Fig.8.2. If
you know the height at which the
person is sitting, can you find the width
of the river?

3. Suppose a hot air balloon is flying in
the air.  A girl happens to spot the
balloon in the sky and runs to her
mother to tell her about it.  Her mother
rushes out of the house to look at the
balloon.Now when the girl had spotted
the balloon intially it was at point A.
When both the mother and daughter
came out to see it, it had already
travelled to another point B. Can you
find the altitude of B from the ground?
In all the situations given above, the distances or heights can be found by using
some mathematical techniques, which come under a branch of mathematics called
‘trigonometry’. The word ‘trigonometry’ is derived from the Greek words ‘tri’
(meaning three), ‘gon’ (meaning sides) and ‘metron’ (meaning measure). In fact,
trigonometry is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle.
The earliest known work on trigonometry was recorded in Egypt and Babylon. Early
astronomers used it to find out the distances of the stars and planets from the Earth.
Even today, most of the technologically advanced methods used in Engineering and
Physical Sciences are based on trigonometrical concepts.
In this chapter, we will study some ratios of the sides of a right triangle with
respect to its acute angles, called trigonometric ratios of the angle. We will restrict
our discussion to acute angles only. However, these  ratios can be extended to other
angles also. We will also define the trigonometric ratios for angles of measure 0° and
90°. We will calculate trigonometric ratios for some specific angles and establish
some identities involving these ratios, called trigonometric identities.

Let's begin with a word that might sound a little scary at first, but is actually quite friendly once you get to know it: trigonometry. The word comes from three Greek words. 'Tri' means three, 'gon' means sides, and 'metron' means measure. So put together, trigonometry simply means the measure of three sides, or more precisely, the study of the relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle. And the star of the show in this chapter is the right triangle, the one with a perfect square corner of ninety degrees.

Now why should you care about any of this? Think about everyday situations. Imagine your class visits a tall monument, like the Qutub Minar. You stand on the ground and look up at the very top. If you draw a line from your eyes to the top, and another line straight along the ground, and the tall monument standing upright, you've imagined a right triangle in the air. Here's the magic question: can you figure out how tall that monument is without climbing it or stretching a giant measuring tape up its side? The answer is yes, using trigonometry.

Here's another picture. A girl sits on her balcony beside a river, looking down at a flower pot on the far bank. The height she's sitting at, plus the angle she looks down, forms a right triangle that lets her work out the width of the river without ever crossing it. Or picture a hot air balloon drifting across the sky. By looking at angles from the ground, you could even find how high up the balloon is.

Notice the common thread in all these stories. In each one, there's some distance or height that's hard or impossible to measure directly, but easy to find if you understand how the sides and angles of a right triangle connect to each other. That's the whole power of trigonometry, and it's not new. The earliest work on it was recorded long ago in Egypt and Babylon, and early astronomers used it to measure distances to stars and planets. Even today, engineers and scientists rely on it constantly.

In this chapter, we'll study special ratios of the sides of a right triangle, taken with respect to its acute angles. These are called trigonometric ratios. We'll mostly stick to acute angles, but we'll also define these ratios for zero degrees and ninety degrees, calculate them for some specific angles, and discover neat relationships called trigonometric identities.

Let's get to the heart of trigonometry. Imagine a right triangle, and pick one of its acute angles — say angle A. The three sides now get special names that depend on where you're standing, on angle A. The side that faces angle A, the one directly across from it, is called the side opposite. The longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. And the remaining side, the one touching angle A that isn't the hypotenuse, is called the side adjacent. Here's something important: if you switched your attention to the other acute angle, the opposite and adjacent sides would swap roles. The names depend on which angle you're looking at.

Now we build ratios out of these sides, and we call them trigonometric ratios. The sine of angle A is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. The cosine of A is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse. The tangent of A is the opposite divided by the adjacent. Then we have three more that are simply the upside-down versions: cosecant is one over sine, secant is one over cosine, and cotangent is one over tangent. A neat fact to notice: tangent of A equals sine of A divided by cosine of A, and cotangent is the reverse, cosine over sine.

Now here's the big, beautiful idea. You might worry that these ratios change if you draw a bigger or smaller triangle. They don't. As long as the angle stays the same, the ratios stay the same. Why? Because triangles with equal angles are similar, and similar triangles have proportional sides. So the sine of a forty degree angle is the same number whether your triangle is tiny or huge. The ratio belongs to the angle, not to the size of the triangle.

A couple of cautions. When we write sine A, the word sine isn't being multiplied by A — it's just shorthand for the sine of angle A. And because the hypotenuse is always the longest side, sine and cosine can never be bigger than one. Finally, if you know just one of these six ratios, you can find all the others. You set the two known sides as multiples of some number k, use the Pythagoras theorem to get the third side, and then read off every ratio you want.

topics.our_understanding:
In this section we figure out the exact values of the trigonometric ratios for some special angles, namely zero degrees, thirty degrees, forty-five degrees, sixty degrees, and ninety degrees. These come up so often that it's worth knowing them by heart, but the beautiful thing is we don't just memorize them, we build them from geometry.

Let's start with forty-five degrees. Imagine a right triangle where one of the other angles is forty-five degrees. Since the three angles add to one hundred eighty, and one is ninety, the remaining two must each be forty-five. So both legs are equal in length. If we call each leg a, then by the Pythagoras theorem the hypotenuse is the square root of two times a. From this, sine of forty-five is one over the square root of two, cosine of forty-five is also one over the square root of two, and tangent of forty-five is one.

Next, for thirty and sixty degrees, we use an equilateral triangle, where every angle is sixty degrees. If we drop a perpendicular from the top vertex straight down, it cuts the triangle into two equal right triangles. Each one has a thirty-degree angle at the top and a sixty-degree angle at the bottom. If the full side is two a, then the half-base is a, and using the Pythagoras theorem the height comes out as the square root of three times a. From this we read off all the ratios for thirty and sixty degrees.

For zero and ninety degrees, we use a clever limiting idea. Picture the angle A shrinking toward zero. The opposite side gets tiny while the hypotenuse nearly equals the adjacent side. So sine of zero is zero and cosine of zero is one. Now swing the other way, letting A grow toward ninety. Now sine of ninety is one and cosine of ninety is zero. Notice some ratios, like tangent of ninety, become not defined because we'd be dividing by zero.

A lovely pattern emerges: as the angle climbs from zero to ninety, sine steadily increases from zero up to one, while cosine steadily decreases from one down to zero. Keep that picture in your head, and the whole table makes sense rather than feeling like random numbers to cram.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with what an identity really means. An ordinary equation might only be true for certain values, but an identity is true for every value you plug in. So a trigonometric identity is an equation built from trigonometric ratios that holds for all the angles involved. That's what makes it so powerful — once you know it's an identity, you can use it anywhere.

Now here's where it all begins. Picture a right triangle, right-angled at B, with sides we'll call AB, BC, and the hypotenuse AC. By the Pythagoras theorem, AB squared plus BC squared equals AC squared. This single fact is the seed for everything.

Watch what happens when we divide every term by AC squared. The ratio AB over AC is cosine of A, and BC over AC is sine of A. So we get cosine squared A plus sine squared A equals one. That's our first and most famous identity, and it's true for every angle from zero up to ninety degrees.

Now divide the same Pythagoras equation by AB squared instead. This time you get one plus tangent squared A equals secant squared A. It works for zero degrees, but tangent and secant aren't defined at ninety degrees, so it holds up to but not including ninety.

Finally, divide by BC squared and you get cotangent squared A plus one equals cosecant squared A. Since cosecant and cotangent aren't defined at zero degrees, this one holds for all angles above zero up to ninety.

Why do we care? Because if you know just one trigonometric ratio, these identities let you find all the others. For instance, if tangent of A is one over root three, then cotangent is root three, and using one plus tangent squared equals secant squared you can work out secant, cosine, sine, and cosecant in turn. Everything connects.

The rest of this section is about proving statements using these three identities. The trick is almost always the same: convert everything into sines and cosines, or into secants and tangents, and then simplify one side until it equals the other. Notice how often the expression one minus sine squared quietly becomes cosine squared, or how multiplying by a clever conjugate clears things up. These identities are your toolkit, and proving things with them is just learning to reach for the right tool.

This is the summary of everything we explored in trigonometry, so let's pull the big ideas together and make sure they feel solid in your mind. Imagine a right triangle, with the right angle sitting at one corner. Once you pick one of the other angles to focus on, every side of that triangle gets a name relative to that angle. The side directly across from your angle is the opposite side, the side touching your angle that isn't the longest one is the adjacent side, and the longest side, across from the right angle, is the hypotenuse. From just these three sides we build our first three ratios. The sine of the angle is the opposite side divided by the hypotenuse. The cosine is the adjacent side divided by the hypotenuse. And the tangent is the opposite side divided by the adjacent side. That's the heart of it.

Now, three more ratios are simply the flips, or reciprocals, of these. Cosecant is one divided by sine. Secant is one divided by cosine. And cotangent is one divided by tangent. There's also a neat shortcut: tangent equals sine divided by cosine, and cotangent equals cosine divided by sine.

Here's a powerful idea to hold onto. If you know just one of these ratios for an acute angle, you can figure out all the others. You're never stuck with only one piece of information. Notice too that sine and cosine can never be bigger than one, because the opposite or adjacent side can never be longer than the hypotenuse. On the other hand, secant and cosecant are always one or larger, since they're the flips of those small numbers.

We also memorized the exact values of these ratios for the special angles zero degrees, thirty degrees, forty-five degrees, sixty degrees, and ninety degrees. Those come up again and again, so they're worth knowing by heart.

Finally, there are three beautiful identities that are always true. Sine squared plus cosine squared equals one. Secant squared minus tangent squared equals one. And cosecant squared equals one plus cotangent squared. These let you connect the ratios to each other and simplify tricky expressions. Take a moment to let all of this settle, because these few rules unlock a huge amount of problem solving.

questions.q_text: A girl sits on her balcony beside a river and looks down at a flower pot on the far bank. Explain how the situation forms a right triangle and what trigonometry allows her to find without crossing the river.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the three lines involved. The height at which the girl sits forms a vertical line going straight down to the ground level (one side of the triangle). Step 2: The horizontal distance from the base of her balcony across to the flower pot on the far bank forms a second side. Step 3: The line of sight from her eyes down to the flower pot forms the third side, the slanted line. Step 4: Since the vertical drop and the horizontal ground meet at a perfect ninety-degree corner, these three lines together make a right triangle. Step 5: She knows the height she is sitting at and the angle at which she looks down (the angle of depression). Using the trigonometric relationship between this angle and the sides, she can calculate the horizontal distance, which is the width of the river. So trigonometry lets her find the river's width without ever crossing it.

questions.q_text: In a right triangle, the sine of angle A equals three fifths. Find the cosine and tangent of angle A.
questions.answer: Sine of A equals opposite divided by hypotenuse, and we are given this is three fifths. So set the opposite side as 3k and the hypotenuse as 5k, where k is some positive number. Use the Pythagoras theorem to find the adjacent side: hypotenuse squared equals opposite squared plus adjacent squared. So (5k) squared equals (3k) squared plus adjacent squared, giving 25k squared equals 9k squared plus adjacent squared. Therefore adjacent squared equals 16k squared, so the adjacent side equals 4k. Now read off the ratios. Cosine of A equals adjacent divided by hypotenuse, which is 4k over 5k, equal to four fifths. Tangent of A equals opposite divided by adjacent, which is 3k over 4k, equal to three fourths. So cosine of A is four fifths and tangent of A is three fourths.

questions.q_text: Starting from an equilateral triangle with each side of length two a, show how dropping a perpendicular from the top vertex lets us find sine of thirty degrees and sine of sixty degrees.
questions.answer: Begin with an equilateral triangle, every angle sixty degrees, each side of length two a. Drop a perpendicular from the top vertex to the base. This perpendicular bisects the base, so each half of the base has length a, and it also bisects the top angle, giving thirty degrees on each side. We now have a right triangle with a thirty-degree angle at the top, a sixty-degree angle at the bottom, a base of length a, and a hypotenuse of length two a. Using the Pythagoras theorem, the height equals the square root of (two a squared minus a squared), which is the square root of (four a squared minus a squared), equal to the square root of three a squared, which is the square root of three times a. Now for the sixty-degree angle at the bottom: the opposite side is the height (square root of three times a) and the hypotenuse is two a, so sine of sixty is (square root of three times a) divided by two a, equals square root of three over two. For the thirty-degree angle at the top: the opposite side is the base a, and the hypotenuse is two a, so sine of thirty is a divided by two a, equals one half.

questions.q_text: If tangent of A equals one over root three, use the trigonometric identities to find cotangent A, secant A, cosine A, sine A, and cosecant A.
questions.answer: Start with tangent A = 1/root3. Cotangent A is the reciprocal of tangent, so cotangent A = root3. Now use one plus tangent squared A = secant squared A. Tangent squared A = (1/root3) squared = 1/3. So secant squared A = 1 + 1/3 = 4/3. Taking the positive root (angle between 0 and 90), secant A = 2/root3. Cosine A is the reciprocal of secant, so cosine A = root3/2. Next use cosine squared A + sine squared A = 1. Cosine squared A = 3/4, so sine squared A = 1 - 3/4 = 1/4, giving sine A = 1/2. Finally cosecant A is the reciprocal of sine, so cosecant A = 2. In summary: cotangent A = root3, secant A = 2/root3, cosine A = root3/2, sine A = 1/2, cosecant A = 2.

questions.q_text: Prove that one minus sine squared A, all divided by cosine A, equals cosine A.
questions.answer: Take the left-hand side: (1 - sine squared A) / cosine A. From the identity cosine squared A + sine squared A = 1, we can rearrange to get 1 - sine squared A = cosine squared A. Substitute this into the numerator: the expression becomes cosine squared A / cosine A. Cancel one factor of cosine A from numerator and denominator, leaving cosine A. This equals the right-hand side, so the identity is proven.

questions.q_text: For an acute angle, the sine equals three divided by five. Find the cosine and the tangent of that angle.
questions.answer: Start with the identity sine squared plus cosine squared equals one. Sine is three-fifths, so sine squared is nine over twenty-five. Then cosine squared equals one minus nine over twenty-five, which is twenty-five over twenty-five minus nine over twenty-five, giving sixteen over twenty-five. Taking the positive square root (since the angle is acute), cosine equals four divided by five. Tangent equals sine divided by cosine, which is (three-fifths) divided by (four-fifths). The fifths cancel, leaving three divided by four. So cosine is four-fifths and tangent is three-fourths.
